name: Abducens nerve palsy and its false-localizing value
presentation: A patient develops horizontal double vision that is worse when looking to one side and at distance, and turns the head toward that side to avoid it. The affected eye cannot abduct past the midline, or does so incompletely, while all other movements are normal. In one patient the cause is a diabetic microvascular lesion that recovers; in another, headache and papilledema reveal raised intracranial pressure from a tumor nowhere near the pons.

deficits.sign: Abduction deficit with esotropia greatest on gaze to the affected side and at distance
Head turned toward the affected side

reasoning: The abducens nerve leaves the pontomedullary junction and runs the longest intracranial course of any cranial nerve, ascending the clivus in the subarachnoid space, bending sharply over the petrous apex beneath the petroclinoid ligament to enter Dorello's canal, and running through the body of the cavernous sinus to the lateral rectus. It is uncrossed, so an abduction deficit is on the side of the nerve. That long vertical course and the sharp bend at the petrous ridge make it the nerve most vulnerable to any process that shifts the brainstem downward or raises intracranial pressure, so a sixth nerve palsy, especially if bilateral, is a classic false-localizing sign that must not be taken to mean pontine disease. A nuclear lesion is recognized because the nucleus also contains the interneurons for the contralateral medial rectus, so nuclear damage causes a conjugate gaze palsy rather than an isolated abduction deficit, usually with an ipsilateral facial palsy from the overlying facial genu. In the cavernous sinus the nerve lies medially beside the carotid artery with the oculosympathetic fibers briefly attached, so a sixth nerve palsy with an ipsilateral Horner syndrome points to the sinus; at the petrous apex it is accompanied by facial pain and deafness in Gradenigo syndrome.

imagingFindings.finding: Papilledema correlates: distended optic nerve sheaths, flattened posterior globes, partially empty sella; mass, venous thrombosis or IIH as the cause.
Enhancing chordoma, meningioma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma or cavernous sinus mass along the nerve's course.
Demyelination or infarct at the facial colliculus giving a gaze palsy rather than an isolated palsy.

commonCauses: Raised intracranial pressure of any cause
Clival tumor, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, cavernous sinus disease

mimics.name: Thyroid eye disease (medial rectus restriction)
mimics.howToDistinguish: Abduction limited by a tight medial rectus; forced duction positive; proptosis

mimics.name: Duane syndrome
mimics.howToDistinguish: Congenital; globe retraction and narrowing of the fissure on adduction

mimics.name: Convergence spasm
mimics.howToDistinguish: Miosis on attempted lateral gaze; functional

management: Examine the fundi for papilledema in every sixth nerve palsy; image if present, bilateral, young, or with any other sign
Isolated palsy in a vasculopath over 50: observe for recovery at 3 months
Prism or occlusion for diplopia; botulinum toxin to the medial rectus in persistent cases

imagingHint.label: abducens nerve rising from the pontomedullary junction along the clivus
